title: Georgia GOP candidate Rick Jackson faces an immigration scandal at his company - CNN
description:
But it exposes a striking contrast between the business practices of a company Jackson owns and the hardline immigration agenda of his campaign.
Jackson, meanwhile, is campaigning to help President Donald Trump tighten the immigration system his company relies on.
Jackson Healthcare has amassed powerful allies.
The legal costs Avant would incur after Jackson Healthcare took over would prove far more consequential.
Allegations of trafficking foreign nurses Nurses Latoya Lewis and Lucinda Byron saw Avant as a ticket to new lives in the United States.
text:
As billionaire Republican Rick Jackson blanketed Georgia’s airwaves this spring with ads vowing a crackdown on undocumented immigrants if elected governor, a company in his healthcare empire was in the throes of a costly legal battle over the treatment of its immigrant workforce.

A lawsuit filed by foreign-born nurses accused Avant Healthcare Professionals of luring them to the United States with the promise of the American Dream, only to pay them substandard wages and trap them in rigid contracts for years. According to their lawsuit, when they tried to quit, Avant threatened to contact Immigration and Customs Enforcement and sought to charge them five-figure fees for leaving.

“Avant’s ‘employment’ is essentially indentured servitude,” the plaintiffs wrote in their complaint.

Avant denied wrongdoing. But on June 22 — days after Jackson became the GOP nominee for governor — the company agreed to a settlement that would give more than 5,000 current and former immigrant workers a share of a $3 million payout and waive unpaid fees.

Until now, the case against Avant has received scant attention and has not previously surfaced in Georgia’s race for governor. But it exposes a striking contrast between the business practices of a company Jackson owns and the hardline immigration agenda of his campaign.

Avant, which specializes in recruiting foreign nurses for jobs at US hospitals, has faced legal scrutiny over its business model and has at times clashed with the Trump administration over its immigration policies. Jackson, meanwhile, is campaigning to help President Donald Trump tighten the immigration system his company relies on.

At times, Jackson’s campaign and his business have struck different tones on immigration. For example, in a campaign ad that helped fuel his political rise this spring, Jackson looks directly at the camera and says, “I don’t care if you’re a Muslim or a Mongolian. You don’t have the right to force your culture on our country.”

But in a corporate guide to navigating culture shock in the US, Avant tells its foreign workers, “You don’t have to choose between the culture you came from and the one you’re adapting to. Finding harmony between the two creates a well-rounded, multicultural identity that enhances both your personal and professional life.”

Jackson’s primary victory stunned his party by toppling the state’s Trump-backed lieutenant governor. He now faces Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, in one of the most anticipated gubernatorial contests of the year. (Bottoms is a former CNN contributor.)

In a statement to CNN, campaign spokesman Garrison Douglas said that Jackson’s focus is on “criminal illegal immigration and following the law.”

“Avant nurses come to America legally, waiting several years, learn English, pay taxes and save lives,” he said. “Avant entered into the settlement to avoid the cost of litigation, allowing the company to focus entirely on bridging critical nursing shortages by connecting the U.S. healthcare system with qualified nurses.”

Jackson’s campaign did not answer questions from CNN regarding his views on legal immigration, including whether he supports additional visas for foreign workers.

Jessica Lacy, a spokeswoman for Avant parent company Jackson Healthcare, emphasized that the court in this case did not find that the company’s business practices were unlawful and the settlement dismissed the claims against Avant with prejudice.

Similar to Jackson’s campaign, Lacy said, “Avant entered into this settlement to avoid the cost and distraction of continued litigation and to remain focused on our mission of supporting healthcare organizations, healthcare professionals and the patients they serve.”

A swift political rise

Jackson, 72, is a titan in the booming healthcare staffing industry, a business centered on supplying hospitals and clinics with medical workers. He founded Jackson Healthcare in 2000, and it now sits atop a network of roughly 20 companies that specialize in recruiting and placing hospital and clinic positions ranging from nurses and physicians to administrators and front desk staff.

Jackson Healthcare has amassed powerful allies. Its advisory board includes ex-Florida Gov. Jeb Bush and Tom Price, the former Georgia congressman who served as Trump’s first Secretary of Health and Human Services. The company became a key player in Georgia’s response to the Covid-19 crisis, racking up about $1 billion in no-bid nursing contracts, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

Jackson’s business success is central to his pitch to voters. His campaign website traces his path from growing up in Georgia’s foster care system to leading a $3 billion healthcare conglomerate that works in all 50 states.

“Rick doesn’t share that to brag — he shares it because his life has always been about action and impact,” the site says.

Florida-based Avant Healthcare Professionals is a relatively recent addition to Jackson’s sprawling business portfolio. Jackson Healthcare called Avant “a pioneer in the field of international recruitment and placement of healthcare professionals” when it acquired the company in 2018. Business records filed in Florida list Rick Jackson as Avant’s manager.

Even before it was purchased, Avant faced legal scrutiny over its preference for foreign labor.

The US Department of Justice alleged in 2013 that Avant discriminated against American workers through job postings that expressed favoritism toward foreign workers, a potential violation of the Immigration and Nationality Act. In a settlement that year, Avant vowed to change its hiring practices and paid a $27,750 fine.

The legal costs Avant would incur after Jackson Healthcare took over would prove far more consequential.

Allegations of trafficking foreign nurses

Nurses Latoya Lewis and Lucinda Byron saw Avant as a ticket to new lives in the United States. Lewis arrived in 2021 from Jamaica; Byron, originally from St. Vincent and the Grenadines, began working at a South Dakota hospital in 2022.

Both signed multi-year contracts with Avant. According to a lawsuit first filed in 2023, they soon found themselves in an inflexible arrangement where they could take little time off, were paid less than colleagues employed directly by the hospitals and had little opportunity for advancement. They struggled to get by on their wages, the complaint said.

When they tried to quit, Avant warned them they would face fees to recoup the costs of bringing them to the US, the complaint said. Staff allegedly threatened to contact Immigration and Customs Enforcement and misled them into believing that leaving could jeopardize their immigration status. Like many foreign nurses, they arrived on EB3 visas, which come with a green card that generally doesn’t require them to stay with the company that helped bring them to the US.

Avant wanted $41,832 from Byron when she left and had 30 days to pay, the complaint said.

Lawyers for Lewis and Byron argued these contracts and Avant’s efforts to enforce them violated the Trafficking Victims Protection Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act. Lewis and Byron were not available to speak to CNN, their lawyers said.

Avant argued there were substantial costs to recruiting foreign nurses and ensuring their immigration compliance. In seeking to dismiss the case, the company countered that the contracts Byron and Lewis signed were straightforward employer compacts, that they had a right to be made whole and the fact that nurses could — and did — leave Avant was itself evidence that Byron and Lewis were not the victims of forced labor.

A federal judge, however, declined to dismiss the trafficking claims. Last year, the case moved to state court in Florida, where a class action lawsuit took form.

In November, the two sides reached a preliminary settlement after identifying 5,219 current and former Avant health care workers who qualified for the class. Under the agreement, each would be eligible for a chunk of a $3 million payout.

A judge approved the terms of the agreement in July.

Lacy noted that “those who will receive monetary relief, most will receive approximately $500 or less.” Others will have fees waived but no additional payout.

Avant is not the only company to face similar allegations. In 2024, Bloomberg Law identified at least 10 class action lawsuits filed by nurses challenging agreements that required them to repay employers if they quit. Last year, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced her office had secured a $660,000 payout from the firm Advanced Care Staffing for forcing foreign nurses into contracts her office called “exploitative.”

Some labor attorneys have characterized contracts like the ones used by Avant as “stay-or-pay” agreements. States including California and New York have banned them, arguing they often take advantage of the most susceptible workers.

The immigrants that work for these healthcare staffing companies on these contracts are almost exclusively from developing countries, said Rachel Dempsey, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs in the case against Avant. She is also associate director of Towards Justice, a nonprofit law firm that specializes in protecting workers and has handled multiple cases involving immigrant healthcare workers that claim they were mistreated by the companies that brought them to the US.

While Dempsey declined to address the case against Avant, citing the settlement agreement, she said that the salaries generally offered to foreign nurses look attractive on paper for immigrants who have little experience with the cost of living in the US or how much nurses typically make.

“When they get here, they realize it’s not enough to support their families,” she said.

Running as an immigration hardliner

In February, as the settlement by Avant took shape, Jackson jumped into the race for governor. He had just 105 days to make his case to Republican voters in Georgia and spent tens of millions of dollars of his own wealth trying to get recognized.

A provocative anti-immigration commercial helped him stand out. It first aired in March and appeared almost 9,000 times on Georgia television stations, according to AdImpact, which tracks campaign advertising. Staring directly into the camera, Jackson promises that immigrants who break the law on his watch will leave the state “deported or departed.”

His credibility on his immigration stance was challenged during the primary by his opponents after the New York Post published the details of a separate lawsuit filed by a Mexican national injured while working at Jackson’s 47,000-square-foot Georgia mansion. When asked by one of his GOP rivals at a debate whether he has hired immigrants who came to the US unlawfully, Jackson responded: “I don’t know.”

Avant has built its business by recruiting foreigners to move to the US and helping them navigate America’s thorny immigration system. And while Jackson has aligned himself with Trump’s immigration overhaul, Avant has pushed back against it at times.

In 2020, Avant sued the Trump administration over visa delays for workers it was trying to bring into the US from the Philippines. The case was ultimately withdrawn after the visas were approved. Earlier this year, Avant’s leadership described the difficulties it has faced under Trump’s new visa policies and expressed optimism that a lawsuit challenging a new $100,000 fee on H-1B visas would be successful.

“That is a lot of money if we were to bring in the volume of nurses this year under the H1B that we brought in last year,” Lesley Hamilton, Avant’s senior vice president of global operations, said in a March video. “Money that … my brain can’t calculate right now at this minute.”

Jackson’s campaign didn’t respond when asked how he could effectively partner with Trump on immigration when his company is at odds with the administration over some of his visa policies.

Avant argues it’s filling a need. Hospitals across the country are bracing for a workforce shortage in the coming decades. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates there will be about 190,000 openings for registered nurses each year over the next decade.

“Avant supports policies that preserve and strengthen legal immigration pathways for qualified healthcare professionals as an important part of addressing the shortage of U.S. nurses,” Lacy said.

Filling nurse openings with foreign labor recruited by healthcare staffing companies is attractive for hospitals because those workers are typically paid less, Demspey said. But that means American-born and educated nurses are increasingly competing against cheaper labor, she added.

“It brings down wages for everybody,” Dempsey said.

CNN asked Jackson’s campaign whether his company helped US hospitals fill jobs with foreign workers that could go to American nurses at higher wages.

His campaign did not respond.

CNN’s David Wright contributed to this report.

text:
Democratic congressmen from Northern Virginia announced an investigation into recent encounters people had with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that the lawmakers call “ICE brutality.”

U.S. Rep. Don Beyer said his office confirmed at least four of what he calls unjustified, violent encounters with ICE agents just within the past two weeks.

He and U.S. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam introduced the investigation, saying the agents involved should be fired and potentially prosecuted.

“We are announcing an investigation into ICE’s misconduct in partnership with Reps. Subramanyam and [James] Walkinshaw [D-Va.], but also with the Democratic leaders of the Judiciary Committee, the Oversight Committee, and the Homeland Security Committee,” Beyer said.

On Aug. 10, an ICE agent pulled his gun on a U.S. citizen in Falls Church while the two argued through her driver side window. Without evidence, the Department of Homeland Security accused Carolina Molina of trying to run the agents over.

Molina joined the congressmen on Capitol Hill Wednesday.

“They should not be in the position that they are as of now if other citizens and other people are at risk,” she said.

In Arlington County the next day, 45-year-old Jose Mejia says ICE agents used a taser on him and assaulted him during an arrest.

DHS says Mejia is in the country illegally and accused him of attempting to flee the scene, requiring agents to use “necessary force to gain control of the situation.”

According to Mejia's attorney, the violent arrest resulted in injuries to Mejia's face and bleeding and swelling of his brain.

Arlington County’s prosecutor said she instructed local police and Virginia’s attorney general to investigate the incident involving Mejia, saying no one is above the law.

text:
HARBEL, Liberia (AP) — The United States on Thursday carried out its first deportation under an agreement for Liberia to accept up to 1,200 people who are not from the African country, one of the Trump administration’s largest efforts yet to deport people to countries other than their own.

The 20 deportees arrived at Roberts International Airport outside Monrovia.

Deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean, according to Liberian Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah. Liberian Justice Minister Natu Oswald Tweh has said they could seek asylum in the West African country if they wished.

The U.S. State Department declined to answer questions about the Liberia agreement, but said that implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority.” It said it was “unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security.”

The U.S. Homeland Security Department declined to confirm Thursday’s deportations “for operational security reasons” and referred additional questions to the State Department.

Third-country agreements are often shrouded in secrecy. Migrants have been deported to countries they have never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

The Trump administration struck agreements with at least 35 countries to deport people who are from other countries, including Liberia and 13 others in Africa, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a partnership of Refugees International and Human Rights First that relies on public records requests, news reports and other sources. More than 23,000 people have deported to 26 countries under the agreements.

The U.S. State Department previously announced that Liberia agreed to accept deportees who are not from Liberia. But a six-page agreement reached in September 2025 and posted on its website does not say how many or from which countries.

In October 2025, Liberia offered to accept Kilmar Abrego Garcia of El Salvador, who was mistakenly deported to prison in El Salvador. Blocked from sending him to his native country, the Trump administration has vowed to send him to a third county, including Liberia.

Abrego Garcia has said he would agree to be deported to Costa Rica, which has said it will accept him. But the government has so far declined to send him there. Abrego Garcia is fighting deportation to Liberia in a federal lawsuit in Maryland.

title: Home Office guidance confirms that you can, in fact, vary a human rights application
description:
Paragraph 34BB has always been clear that you can vary any application, including a human rights one.
So the Rules clearly do envisage circumstances in which a human rights application can be varied, as this is what the different procedures in this sub-paragraph exemplify.
Despite the fact that the first application is a deemed human rights application, Octavian can absolutely vary the application as he has done and the Skilled Worker application is granted on 14 August 2026.
However, I have never heard of the Home Office deciding an initial, varied human rights claim after the application that this was varied to was refused.
If you have an example of the Home Office deciding an earlier human rights claim after refusing a varied non-human rights application, please do give me a shout.
text:
Paragraph 34BB has always been clear that you can vary any application, including a human rights one. Yet until a few days ago, the ‘Validation, variation, voiding and withdrawal of applications’ guidance stated confusingly that human rights applications could not be varied.

I had long suspected, and I can’t imagine I was the only one, that this was simply a misunderstanding of paragraph 34BB(7) which states that the human rights claim aspect of an initial application still falls to be decided if it is varied to a different application which is then refused:

(7) Where a human rights claim is made as part of an application and a subsequent application is made which varies that application under paragraph 34BB(1), if the applicant is then granted entry clearance or permission to stay, any outstanding human rights claim will be treated as withdrawn, but where any subsequent application is refused, the human rights claim, if not already decided, remains outstanding and will be considered at a time decided by the Secretary of State.

So the Rules clearly do envisage circumstances in which a human rights application can be varied, as this is what the different procedures in this sub-paragraph exemplify. This makes the previously-erroneous guidance even more baffling.

The guidance has now been amended to clarify this point:

Where an applicant has an undecided application for entry clearance or permission to stay, any further application for entry clearance or permission to stay will be treated as an application to vary the previous application. Only the most recent application will be considered.

Where the previous application included a human rights claim, that claim is not automatically extinguished because the application has been varied and you must take action depending on the outcome of the considered application:

if the later application is granted, any outstanding human rights claim will be treated as withdrawn

if the later application is refused, any human rights claim which has not already been decided remains outstanding and will be considered at a time decided by the Secretary of State

Apparently, this amendment took the intervention of the ‘Home Office Legal Advisors’, which is a bit odd given that the Home Office definitely allowed human rights applications to be varied in practice. I’m not sure why anyone required this level of persuasion, particularly since the idea that you couldn’t do this has never had any legal basis.

Either way, the clarity offered by this amendment is great news, even if we don’t expect anything to change in practice.

So how does that work?

Case study

Octavian lodged an in-country unmarried partner application under Appendix FM on 29 June 2026 and had not yet received a decision on the application.

The relationship on which that application was based subsequently broke down so Octavian’s employer, which has a licence to sponsor Skilled Workers, agreed to sponsor him and issued him with a Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS). Octavian used that CoS to vary the outstanding Appendix FM application to a Skilled Worker one on 5 August 2026 by submitting a new form, paying the new fee, uploading the Skilled Worker documents and attending a new biometrics appointment.

Despite the fact that the first application is a deemed human rights application, Octavian can absolutely vary the application as he has done and the Skilled Worker application is granted on 14 August 2026. Because he has varied the Appendix FM application, that first application is no longer in front of the Home Office to decide. Octavian will eventually receive a full refund of the first set of fees, minus a nominal administrative fee.

So what if the variation application is refused?

Paragraph 34BB(7) states that where the first application is a human rights one, and this is varied to another application which is then refused, the human rights claim aspect of this first application can and should still be considered by the Home Office at some point. So how does this work in practice?

Honestly, I have no idea. In the decade that I have worked in this field, I have never seen this happen in practice. I suspect this is because this would only be relevant where the second application is a non-human rights one, as the human rights part of the claim would already be considered as part of the second application’s decision making process.

It is very rare though for someone to vary from a human rights application to a non-human rights application for no reason, because people rarely switch from asking for their generic human rights to be considered to something highly specific like a work or study application unless they have a good reason to think the latter will be granted. In other words, no one makes a speculative Skilled Worker application.

However, I have never heard of the Home Office deciding an initial, varied human rights claim after the application that this was varied to was refused. I am sceptical that this actually happens in practice, at least outside of removal or deportation matters much later. If you have an example of the Home Office deciding an earlier human rights claim after refusing a varied non-human rights application, please do give me a shout. Validity, variation and section 3C stuff is one of my favourite areas of immigration law and I hate not knowing everything about it so you really would be doing me a favour.

In the joint filing by Salt Lake City, Salt Lake County and U.S. Department of Homeland Security officials in the federal lawsuit, the sides acknowledge as much.

text:
SALT LAKE CITY — As has been presumed since June, federal officials have abandoned their plans to build a new immigration detention center in Salt Lake City, according to a federal court filing Wednesday.

In the joint filing by Salt Lake City, Salt Lake County and U.S. Department of Homeland Security officials in the federal lawsuit, the sides acknowledge as much.

"On July 17, 2026, defendants, through counsel, informed plaintiffs that they no longer intend to convert the Salt Lake warehouse into an immigration detention facility and instead intend to designate the Salt Lake facility as excess property for disposition by the General Services Administration ('GSA)," reads the filing. The document was filed as part of the litigants' efforts to get the judge to stay the case, or temporarily pause it.

Salt Lake City and Salt Lake County, the plaintiffs, filed suit in U.S. District Court on June 8 against U.S. Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and other immigration officials, the defendants, to stop the plans. The Salt Lake city and county officials had charged that federal officials didn't follow proper federal procedures in designating the proposed site at 6020 W. 300 South as a detention center.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, purchased the empty warehouse on 300 South for $145.44 million last March for conversion into an immigrant detention center, part of President Donald Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration. The plans sparked an uproar among immigrant advocates and protesting. Then news emerged late in June in a New York Times report that federal officials planned to offload the Salt Lake City site and abandon plans to convert the warehouse into an immigrant detention center.

At the time, DHS didn't directly say the plans in Utah had been abandoned, but hinted at it. "DHS is moving swiftly to utilize EXISTING detention space with our state and county partners," the agency said in a statement last June.

Reps for Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson and Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall declined comment Wednesday as the issue remains in litigation. In response to a KSL query, reps from the Department of Homeland Security issued the same statement the agency provided last June to media outlets when the New York Times report came out.

"From day one, DHS has remained singularly focused on removing the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the United States and is always evaluating the best methods to do so. These heinous criminals, once arrested, should be removed at lightning speed, not housed on American soil at the taxpayer's expense," reads the rehashed statement. The reissued statement also included the line about using "existing" detention center space.

'Hallelujah"

Brent Ward, an attorney who had been involved in separate efforts with a new nonprofit group, Uproar Utah, to sue to halt the plans, welcomed the news.

"All I can say is hallelujah," Ward said. "That's the culmination of the efforts of a lot of people ... behind the scenes, but also the city attorney, the mayor and everybody who applied political pressure in any way, shape or form."

Read more:

The plans had garnered support from some, including Gov. Spencer Cox, but the foes spoke more loudly, at least publicly, in expressing their displeasure with the plans. The critics had variously feared detainees would be mistreated, that the site couldn't adequately house a detention center capable of holding up to 10,000 people, as proposed, and that such a facility didn't fit in the industrial area where it was proposed.

Federal officials never formally responded to the lawsuit. According to the language of the proposed stay, also filed Wednesday, those involved would craft a report more specifically spelling out what happens with the site. The judge in the matter has yet to rule on the request for a stay. The proposed report, if the judge agrees to the language of the stay, would be filed within 60 days.

City and county officials probably don't want the case dismissed "until the property is actually disposed of and the use of the facility as a jail is foreclosed beyond peradventure," Ward said. "So the city wants the court to retain jurisdiction until the door has been completely shut. That is a prudent position."

The Utah Democratic Party issued a statement calling federal officials' plans to abandon the proposal "a retreat" and charging that the process federal officials followed lacked transparency.

"Credit belongs to Democratic leaders like Mayor Erin Mendenhall and Salt Lake County Mayor Jenny Wilson, who stood their ground and made DHS answer for this plan in court instead of behind closed doors," reads the statement. "Complaints of violent incidents, misconduct and wrongful arrests keep piling up against ICE and its response isn't accountability. It's avoidance. That's not an agency we should trust anywhere near our neighbors, our families or our streets."

title: Idaho county probation officers compile 'foreign-born list' to hand over to ICE as critics raise alarms
description:
On June 3, Naranjo told five ICE officers that she would talk to Breach about the "foreign-born list."
Subsequent messages, however, show at least some probation officers used foreign birthplace as a way to identify people for review.
Probation officers were regularly alerting ICE agents about the dates and times that certain probationers would be arriving at their office, according to the emails.
In some cases, probation officers asked ICE if a person who had missed check-ins was in their custody.
One officer also gave ICE agents the home address and make, model and license plate of a probationer’s car.
text:
A southwestern Idaho county's probation officers have been compiling a list of foreign-born people on probation for federal immigration authorities, even though county officers did not independently verify whether everyone identified was in the U.S. illegally.

In Canyon County, Idaho, more than 140 emails between county probation officers and Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from May to July 2026 show how the probation department has coordinated with ICE’s Boise office, including by combing through its case files to create a list of foreign-born people on probation to hand over to ICE, according to communications obtained by InvestigateWest.

In May, a probation officer emailed ICE about a man she would meet the next day for his regular check-in.

"His meeting has not changed and he is expected to be here tomorrow morning at 7:30 a.m.," Norma Naranjo, a senior probation officer for Canyon County’s misdemeanor probation department, wrote in a May 13 email to six ICE agents.

MISSISSIPPI LAW COULD CREATE STATEWIDE REGISTRY OF UNDOCUMENTED IMMIGRANTS

The next day, the man arrived for his appointment a few minutes early, and Naranjo contacted the ICE agents again to ask if they would be coming soon.

"He is here are you guys on your way?" she wrote.

It was unclear from the heavily redacted emails if ICE agents took the man into custody at his probation appointment, according to InvestigateWest.

The list compiled for ICE appeared to have been made without confirming that the people in question are in the country illegally. According to InvestigateWest, one probation officer said in an email that the names he submitted included everyone in his files who had reported being born outside the United States. Foreign birth alone does not indicate unlawful immigration status; foreign-born people can include naturalized U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green-card holders.

Idaho law enforcement agencies have long worked with federal immigration officials to detain illegal immigrants who are in jail or serving their sentence on probation, but immigration attorneys and advocates fear that Canyon County’s foreign-born list could lead to probationers in the country legally being detained, particularly as ICE agents during the Trump administration detained or caught up U.S. citizens and people with lawful or pending immigration status in immigration enforcement actions. Some lawfully present noncitizens, including green card holders, can also be subject to removal based on certain criminal convictions or other grounds under federal law.

Nikki Ramirez-Smith, an immigration attorney with Ramirez-Smith Law in Nampa, Idaho, said the county’s efforts to compile a list of foreign-born people on probation for ICE is "an invasion of privacy."

"It’s one thing to know that someone is "undocumented", it’s another thing to just start targeting every single person who was born in another country," she told InvestigateWest.

Jeff Breach, the director of Canyon County's misdemeanor probation department, said the list includes "individuals whose place of birth is a foreign country — and can also include individuals that have been previously flagged with an immigration hold."

"Verifying and determining legal presence/status, along with any related enforcement, is within the purview of federal authorities," Breach told the outlet.

Breach said ICE has requested a list of people that could be in the country illegally, typically on an annual basis and across administrations. He said the probation department coordinates with ICE the same way it would with any local or state law enforcement agency by providing them "information to carry out their lawful duties."

Steve Cushman, director of constituent services for Canyon County, said he did not know exactly when the lists were first requested and provided, but added that it is his understanding that it goes back as far as the Obama administration.

On June 3, Naranjo told five ICE officers that she would talk to Breach about the "foreign-born list."

"We are working on a procedure to keep a list current for your agency," Naranjo wrote. "I will get back to you on this as soon as we figure something out."

Two days later, Breach sent an email to his staff directing them to compile a list of illegal immigrants.

"ICE has requested a list of offenders who are in the country illegally," he wrote. "I need you to go through your caseload this month and send me a list of names of offenders who you believe are in the country illegally. I’ll review the names and put together a list that can be sent to ICE so that they can look into if the person is in the country illegally and if they want to take any action."

The email shows ICE requested offenders believed to be in the country illegally, rather than all foreign-born probationers. Subsequent messages, however, show at least some probation officers used foreign birthplace as a way to identify people for review.

Most of the emails from May 1 to July 10 are heavily redacted, but they show how probation officers used information in their case files to compile the list.

"That’s everyone in my cabinet that filled out (an) intake form and stated not born in US," Brandon Black, a Canyon County probation officer, said in an email back to Breach on June 8.

Another officer, Justin Donovan, told Breach that he only identified one person under his supervision who "may be here illegally," adding that the man "only had an ID from Mexico during his last arrest."

More than half of the people on the list were on probation for driving under the influence, five people were on probation for drug-related crimes and nine people for disturbing the peace, according to InvestigateWest. Only seven people were identified as having an ICE hold, meaning the federal government had already identified them for potential deportation.

Probation officers were regularly alerting ICE agents about the dates and times that certain probationers would be arriving at their office, according to the emails. In some cases, probation officers asked ICE if a person who had missed check-ins was in their custody. In two instances, officers emailed ICE just before and during the appointments to verify they were on their way to detain a probationer. One officer also gave ICE agents the home address and make, model and license plate of a probationer’s car.

Breach estimated that in the last three months, ICE agents have been at one or two probation appointments per month.

"All the law enforcement agencies we work with prefer to meet with offenders up in the office due to it being a controlled environment, which means it is safer for the offender, the officer, and the public," he wrote. "There is an expectation from law enforcement agencies and the public that probation officers work cooperatively with law enforcement to ensure the safety of all parties involved."

Pressed on whether the department is concerned that U.S. citizens or others with legal status could be included in the list, Breach referred to a previous statement that verifying a person’s status "is within the purview of federal authorities."

"ICE may still target someone if they think the conviction is a deportable or removal offense even if they (have legal) status. Sometimes, ICE doesn’t get that right," Alycia Moss, an immigration attorney with Fennemore Law in Coeur d’Alene, told InvestigateWest, noting that ICE agents should know if someone on the list is deportable or not but may still target people who are in the U.S. legally.

NEW YORKER SUING ICE AFTER OFFICERS WENT TO HIS HOME TO WARN HIM OVER CRITICISM OF AGENCY

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Canyon County has faced criticism in the past for its attempts to help ICE.

In 2019, staff at the Canyon County Sheriff’s Office were told to notify immigration officials of "all foreign-born inmates" who were booked into the jail. Some of the people they alerted agents to were U.S. citizens who had posted bond, according to the Idaho Press. If inmates served jail time and posted bond, staff were directed to contact immigration officials.

That year, Canyon County faced three lawsuits from people who said they were illegally held in jail, despite posting bond, because the county refused to release them over their immigration status. The county settled with at least one man for $13,000.

The sheriff’s office is also facing a lawsuit from the ACLU of Idaho over allegations that the county and other law-enforcement agencies involved in an October 2025 ICE raid racially profiled Latino attendees and unlawfully detained people at a horse-racing venue. The allegations have not been adjudicated.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the county's probation department and ICE for comment.

title: Oped: ICE out of Rhode Island: Say no to terror; Say yes to community!
description:
An oped from the Immigrant Solidarity group of the Providence General Assembly Every month, ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) kidnaps dozens of Rhode Island residents, leaving behind traumatized children and broken families.
No family should ever have to face the cruelty of state terror.
Rhode Island has taken some important steps, but still has a long way to go to protect our immigrant friends and neighbors.
Across the U.S. and right here in little Rhody, ICE has relied on state resources to facilitate its terror.
We are responding to this terror with immigrant solidarity, organizing to protect our friends and neighbors in Providence, in Rhode Island, and in the surrounding areas.
text:
An oped from the Immigrant Solidarity group of the Providence General Assembly

Every month, ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) kidnaps dozens of Rhode Island residents, leaving behind traumatized children and broken families. Nearly 700 Rhode Islanders were taken by ICE in just the first 12 months of the current Trump regime. Every person ICE has seized was part of the fabric of our community: a mother, a father, a cousin, a coworker, a neighbor, a pastor, a mentor, a friend.

While the major enforcement surges in Chicago, Minneapolis, Portland and elsewhere dominated the news, ongoing ICE activity is now much less visible. But whether we see it or not, the grinding machine of deportation has continued quietly and relentlessly, across the country and here in our own backyard.

We saw the real human cost of this in the recent case of Chansareth Hong, a Cambodian refugee who came to Providence as an infant in 1978 and has only ever known our state and this country as home. Despite decades of living in and contributing to our community, despite a long record of complying with immigration check-ins, and despite being the primary caregiver for his elderly mother and nine-year-old autistic son, Hong was detained at a regularly scheduled appointment and thrown into immigration limbo. Our community was relieved to hear that a federal court judge has since ordered him released. No family should ever have to face the cruelty of state terror.

Rhode Island has taken some important steps, but still has a long way to go to protect our immigrant friends and neighbors. We commend the Rhode Island General Assembly and Governor Daniel McKee for recently passed legislation that prohibits ICE from conducting civil immigration arrests at our local courthouses without a judicial warrant, prevents ICE from being within 200 feet of polling places, and enables individuals to sue ICE for civil rights violations. Yet, much more could be done.

Across the U.S. and right here in little Rhody, ICE has relied on state resources to facilitate its terror. From informal information sharing to direct collaboration to crowd control under the guise of “public safety,” state and local police have often provided cover, granting ICE agents the ability to carry out their kidnappings. State and local police have looked the other way when ICE and other federal agents drive recklessly, brandish weapons, make threats, or physically assault people: all crimes under state law. Federal agents have routinely commandeered state resources, making use of state property and community spaces as staging grounds for their assaults on our communities. They have targeted the spaces of everyday life, including schools, hospitals, and churches.

The Trump regime and their white supremacist and Christian nationalist supporters seek to undo every step that oppressed peoples have made towards greater equality and collective liberation. They want a world where liberty means license for the few, and subjugation for others. In service of this vision, they are dehumanizing those they define as a threat or enemy, including immigrants, people of color, and trans people. They are actively rewriting the rules of who belongs by ignoring due process, dismantling asylum, stripping people of legal status, and trying to restrict birthright citizenship. They are trying to normalize the tools and aesthetics of fascism. Masked secret police occupy cities, smash car windows, kill people in the streets, and disappear tens of thousands into an abusive network of concentration camps. They are deporting people to foreign prisons or dropping them off in places they have never been and where they have no connections, sometimes without money, passport, or a change of clothes.

We are responding to this terror with immigrant solidarity, organizing to protect our friends and neighbors in Providence, in Rhode Island, and in the surrounding areas. We are building community power in the face of adversity and mobilizing ourselves where the government fails to keep us safe.

We are standing up for freedom and liberation and working to realize a vision of mutual aid and fundamental dignity for every human being. A vision that embraces the freedom to love, form families, cross borders to escape climate catastrophe and war, to build a future and home free from violence and terror. We reject the Trump regime’s cruelty as well as that of the neoliberal capitalism of the past 50 years. This system has celebrated free markets and imperialism but restricted the free movement of human beings to escape the fallout or pursue their dreams.

While ordinary Rhode Islanders, grassroots organizations, and local mutual aid networks have mobilized to defend our neighbors, we have seen an alarming vacuum of leadership at the state level compared to other states in the region.

Democratic governors in neighboring states like Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Jersey, and New York have taken bold executive action to curtail collaboration with ICE, while Governor Dan McKee has lagged. His primary challenger, Helena Foulkes, has also remained largely silent, offering no comprehensive immigration platform to address this crisis.

Rhode Islanders will not stay silent, and neither should those who occupy or seek the governor’s office. We demand that McKee and Foulkes commit to immediate, concrete action:

No ICE on State Property: Issue an immediate executive order prohibiting ICE and other immigration enforcement agents from using any state-owned property, buildings, parks, beaches, or parking lots as staging areas, processing locations, or operational bases.

No 287(g) Agreements or State Collaboration: Prevent any state agency, state police, or department of corrections personnel from formally or informally collaborating with or facilitating federal immigration enforcement.

Protect Our Public Institutions: Direct state executive agencies to work with public and private institutions, including schools and hospitals, to ensure clear, enforceable policies requiring a judicial warrant to enter nonpublic spaces.

The time for half measures has passed. We call on our state leadership to stand with Rhode Island’s families, reject the politics of terror, and use every tool of executive and legislative power to make Rhode Island truly safe for everyone who calls it home.

Join us! The PGA meets every other Saturday at noon, 134 Mathewson St., Providence

text:
The Colorado attorney general has filed a lawsuit on behalf of the state's public health department seeking to force the company that runs the Aurora ICE Processing Center to comply with a tuberculosis investigation.

The lawsuit comes after state health officials issued an order last week demanding the Aurora ICE Processing Center turn over tuberculosis records the state says the facility has withheld for nearly two months after a detainee tested positive for the disease in June. GEO Group had until Monday to comply with the order and failed to do so, according to the suit.

▶️ Denver7's Colette Bordelon spoke with AG Weiser as well as activists outside the facility Wednesday after the suit was filed

Colorado sues Geo Group over tuberculosis investigation at Aurora ICE facility

"Our public health department deserves access to get the information it needs to assure the public that any threats to public health have been addressed and are no longer a risk. Without GEO Group following the law, they can't do their job," said Attorney General Phil Weiser. "GEO Group has this responsibility. They need to step up, follow the law, and help ensure that we keep all Coloradans safe."

The suit claims the company has "prevented [Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment] and local public health agencies from performing any meaningful and statutorily required disease investigation and control."

"Colorado is therefore flying in the dark when it comes to a contagious and deadly infectious disease within its borders," CDPHE claims in the suit. "Just-take-our-word-for-it is not a viable public health response to such a disease."

Read Denver7's previous coverage below:

Colorado health officials order Aurora ICE Processing Center to hand over tuberculosis records

State health dept gives GEO Group until Friday to allow tuberculosis investigation at Aurora ICE facility

CDPHE fields questions about Aurora ICE facility TB investigation as groups demand more state action

Health officials confirm TB case at Aurora ICE facility; ICE says person has been 'removed from the county'

After a late June order from Adams County Public Health, the company provided "some information, such as staff and detainee lists," and began attending weekly calls with the Adams County Health Department to monitor the case, according to the court filing.

GEO Group stopped communicating directly with Adams County Health Department and stopped attending the meetings around July 1, requesting all further communication to go through the company's lawyers, according to the suit.

"These communications did not result in the production of any meaningful information," the filing states.

According to the lawsuit, the company provided no information about the infected detainee's medical history, how many people in the facility had been in contact with that detainee, whether those people had been tested for TB and whether contact tracing was occurring.

State health officials issued a letter to the facility July 14, and the governor's office made two additional requests on July 17 and July 20, according to the suit and previous Denver7 reporting. State officials continued to try to gain more information over the next several weeks.

"In response, state officials received no meaningful information that would allow CDPHE to conduct its disease control duties," the suit claims.

After the GEO Group's "persistent stonewalling," state health officials issued a public health order Aug. 13, per the filing.

The company has historically worked with public health officials to provide access to the facility for disease control investigations, according to the suit.

"We are disappointed that GEO’s refusal to comply has made legal action necessary, particularly because Colorado public health officials have successfully collaborated with GEO on communicable disease investigations in the past," a CDPHE spokesperson said in a statement to Denver7.

"We remain ready to work collaboratively, but cooperation requires GEO to provide information required by law," the statement continued. "We hope this action results in prompt compliance so public health officials can successfully complete the investigation and ensure that anyone who may have been exposed receives appropriate notification, testing and follow-up care."

GEO Group did not respond to Denver7's request for comment by the time of publication, but ICE officials have previously claimed that there are no active cases of TB at the facility and that the person who tested positive in June has since been "treated, cleared, and removed from the country."

"Even if true, this does not end the public health emergency," the state's court filing claims "If anything, it makes the need to obtain information from the facility even more pressing, because CDPHE’s ability to conduct its investigation only becomes harder with the passage of time."

TB is an airborne and potentially fatal disease that can cause severe lung damage and can spread to other organs, according to health officials. It is curable with treatment, but "may result in permanent disability or death" if left untreated, health officials have said.

"Prompt identification of exposed individuals is critical to preventing additional illness," officials said in a previous release about the TB case at the Aurora ICE facility.

Health officials' inability to properly conduct an investigation endangers detainees, staff and the general public, according to the suit.

“The GEO Group is endangering Coloradans’ public health by refusing to follow the state health department’s order and by violating Colorado law," Attorney General Weiser said in a statement. "This law keeps our residents safe and enables the health department to take necessary measures to prevent the spread of infectious diseases like tuberculosis. We will continue to defend Colorado law and ensure that no company flouts our public health and safety laws.”

Gov. Jared Polis said in a statement he is "hopeful the courts will ensure that local public health officials get the information needed to protect public health.”

"The State and public health officials simply want to conduct a routine public health investigation to protect the health of our fellow Coloradans and GEO’s consistent lack of transparency has kept that from happening," he said in the statement.

title: Court ruled against immigration authorities. Here's what changed in Idaho
description:
This provision provided bond hearings, where immigrants who were not a “danger, security threat or flight risk” could be released, according to a 2025 Idaho court order.
People swept up under the new policy were “trapped” in detention, the 2025 Idaho court order said.
In Idaho, one immigrant subjected to mandatory detention had an active visa petition and another had a work permit and a pending asylum application.
The issue has split circuit courts, with the 9th Circuit (which Idaho is part of) and six other circuit courts rejecting the administration’s position.
The Department of Homeland Security said it was confident in its legal position about mandatory detention, according to a spokesperson.
text:
A divided three-person panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in July sided with immigrants against the Trump administration’s expansion of mandatory detention, which has left many immigrants detained without a bond hearing.

But the effect on Idaho immigrants is mixed after the ruling, local immigration lawyers told the Statesman, even with the 9th Circuit finding that some immigrants are eligible for bond hearings. That’s because immigration lawyers worry people won’t get a fair shake thanks to frequent denials of bond.

“In some ways it is worse,” said Jacob Rourk, attorney at Ramirez-Smith Law. “Even if it feels hotter, like we’ve jumped out of the frying pan and into the fire, I still think that we are making progress.”

At issue is the Trump administration’s push for mandatory detention, which lies in two sections of federal statute.

The first, which has applied to people seeking entry to the U.S. at the border, generally requires agents to detain someone if it’s unclear whether they are eligible to enter.

The second, which has applied to immigrants already in the U.S. in deportation proceedings, says detention is allowed but not required. This provision provided bond hearings, where immigrants who were not a “danger, security threat or flight risk” could be released, according to a 2025 Idaho court order.

But the Trump administration, as part of its expansive crackdown on immigrants, has tried a new tactic: detaining people without a bond hearing under the first provision, even if the immigrant has lived in the U.S. for a long time. People swept up under the new policy were “trapped” in detention, the 2025 Idaho court order said.

In Idaho, one immigrant subjected to mandatory detention had an active visa petition and another had a work permit and a pending asylum application.

Now though, lawyers say their clients are still being detained, and even if they can get a bond hearing, it may not be fair.

Immigration judges work for the Department of Justice, and such courts are administrative. Since he took office, the Trump administration has pressured immigration judges to deport more people, according to the New York Times. Immigration judges are under pressure to deny bond, according to Politico.

The Department of Justice and Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not return requests for comment. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in an email that the agency “strongly” disagreed with the 9th Circuit’s ruling.

“This legal position was the nail in the coffin for Biden’s catch and release policies,” the spokesperson wrote. “That is why the left and their activist proxies on the judiciary are resisting it so vigorously. President Trump and (Homeland Security) Secretary (Markwayne) Mullin are now enforcing the law as it was actually written to keep America safe.”

What changed after the ruling?

Since the ruling, Immigration and Customs Enforcement is declaring people a danger or flight risk to detain them, regardless of whether that’s true, Rourk said.

And local immigration lawyers say that even if an immigrant can get a bond hearing, that hearing might be unfair.

The immigration judges in Tacoma, whom many Idaho immigrants go before, granted bond in 3% of cases in fiscal year 2023, the lowest bond rate in the U.S., according to a court order in the original lawsuit preceding the 9th Circuit’s decision.

“They will deny anybody for any reason they can possibly muster,” Rourk said in a phone interview.

John Shackelford, owner-operator of a Boise-based law firm, echoed concerns about unfair bond hearings.

In one case, U.S. District Judge B. Lynn Winmill released an Idaho immigrant after what he called a “rubberstamp” denial. The immigrant provided scores of evidence at a bond hearing, including his U.S. citizen children’s birth certificates, his tax filings and letters of support from community members. The government submitted only a 2022 form, and the immigration judge used evidence not in the record to make a decision and didn’t record the hearing.

Still, Shackelford said more lawyers are able to work with immigrants on their bond hearings than with the habeas cases challenging mandatory detention, making help more readily available.

“I think (the 9th Circuit ruling) is a good thing,” he said.

What did the 9th Circuit say?

The 9th Circuit opinion, written by Judge Daniel Bress, a Trump-nominated judge, said that undocumented immigrants who are already in the country when they are apprehended are not subject to mandatory detention.

In the opinion, Bress pointed to the long history of treating immigrants at the border differently than those immigrants who are already in the U.S.

Since the close of the 19th century, immigrants arriving in the U.S. who don’t seem eligible to enter have been subject to mandatory detention, the opinion said, but in the early 20th century, Congress allowed some immigrants in the U.S. a chance for release on bond.

The U.S. Supreme Court, in a separate 2018 decision, had already explained that same concept: mandatory detention at the border but not for people already here in the country, the opinion said.

Through five presidential administrations (Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden and Trump’s first term), immigration officials have carried out those two statutes since the 1996 amendments to the statutes. Immigration officials have adhered to those two concepts: detention for some at the border, but not necessarily for those already in the U.S.

“We are aided by the further common-sense intuition that a change of this magnitude would likely not have gone unnoticed and unobserved in the nearly thirty years since it was allegedly put into place,” the 2026 9th Circuit opinion said.

What comes next?

The hardening of the administration toward all immigrants, undocumented or not, has trickled down to Idaho. Immigration agents have waited at the airport and changed their tactics, including smashing car windows to get at people. Some Idaho immigrants have been hit with million-dollar plus fines for being in the U.S. after a deportation order, even if they’d already left the country or officials had decided not to remove them.

The 9th Circuit’s decision isn’t set in stone. The U.S. Supreme Court is expected to rule on the issue of mandatory detention, said Matt Adams, legal director with the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, which brought the original suit leading to the 9th Circuit’s decision.

The issue has split circuit courts, with the 9th Circuit (which Idaho is part of) and six other circuit courts rejecting the administration’s position. Only the 5th and the 8th circuits have ruled in favor of the government, according to Politico.

The Department of Homeland Security said it was confident in its legal position about mandatory detention, according to a spokesperson.

“As our record in the U.S. Supreme Court demonstrates, the law is on our side,” the spokesperson said.

The Trump administration uses detention as an “extreme deterrent and punishment,” Adams said, and many people just give up on their cases because of the toll of being locked up indefinitely.

“It’s very hard for people,” Adams said.

text:
Updated Aug. 19, 2026, at 9:46 p.m.

Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser filed a lawsuit Wednesday against GEO Group after the publicly traded company failed to comply with a state public health order over at least one case of tuberculosis at an immigrant detection facility in Aurora.

“The GEO Group is endangering Coloradans’ public health by refusing to follow the state health department’s order and by violating Colorado law,” Weiser, a Democrat who is running for governor, said in a press release. “This law keeps our residents safe and enables the health department to take necessary measures to prevent the spread of infectious diseases like tuberculosis. We will continue to defend Colorado law and ensure that no company flouts our public health and safety laws.”

The move comes after weeks of what state and local public health officials have described as stonewalling by the company and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement over a required public health investigation after a TB case was confirmed at the Aurora ICE Processing Center in June.

Order issued last week

Last week, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment issued a public health order after GEO didn’t provide the state with “medical information, potential contacts, and detainee discharge and transfer information” for the state investigation of tuberculosis at the Aurora facility.

GEO missed the Monday deadline.

CPR reached out to GEO Group, which is based in Florida, and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. GEO Group has not yet responded. ICE referred questions to the Department of Homeland Security. It has not yet responded.

The release notes that under Colorado law, “it is unlawful” to violate a public health order.

The lawsuit was filed in Adams County District Court. It requests the court to issue an injunction to stop the GEO Group’s “stonewalling of the state’s tuberculosis investigation,” the release said and to protect the public health of Coloradans from a contagious and deadly disease.

TB is curable, but can be fatal if not treated

Tuberculosis, or TB, is a highly contagious bacterial disease. Untreated, it can be fatal. Immigration detention facilities are at an even higher risk of TB. They often hold people who recently traveled from counties with an increased prevalence of it.

Staff members, who return to their homes and communities, can further spread TB, if they were to contract it.

“Despite confirming that a detainee of the facility tested positive for tuberculosis, the GEO Group has prevented CDPHE and local public health agencies from performing any meaningful and statutorily required disease investigation and control,” states the suit. “Instead, the GEO Group asked Colorado to put blind-faith into the facility’s response to the disease.”

The suit said Colorado is “flying in the dark when it comes to a contagious and deadly infectious disease within its borders. Just-take-our-word-for-it is not a viable public health response to such a disease.”

Governor, health officials respond

“The state and public health officials simply want to conduct a routine public health investigation to protect the health of our fellow Coloradans and GEO’s consistent lack of transparency has kept that from happening,” said Gov. Jared Polis, in an emailed statement.

He noted the state made “repeated requests for GEO to work with local partners," like the Adams County Public Health Department, which issued its own public health order after the case was first confirmed in June. Polis, a Democrat, said he appreciated collaborating with Weiser’s office on the situation.

“I am hopeful the courts will ensure that local public health officials get the information needed to protect public health,” he said

The state health department issued a press release, saying “we strongly support the attorney general’s legal action to enforce the public health order and uphold the state’s authority and responsibility to protect public health.”

The agency added it is “disappointed that GEO’s refusal to comply has made legal action necessary, particularly because Colorado public health officials have successfully collaborated with GEO on communicable disease investigations in the past.”

“We hope this is a meaningful path to enforcement,” said Kelly Weidenbach, the executive director of the Adams County Health Department. “We believe state leadership is appropriate because the issues at stake extend beyond Adams County and concern the integrity of Colorado’s public health system and its ability to protect people from infectious disease.”

More reaction

“We applaud the attorney general’s demand that GEO obey the standard rules of public health,” said Sen. John Hickenlooper, a Democrat, in an email. “GEO officials are not convincing when they say their lawyers won’t allow them to explain what they did to address a live tuberculosis case in the Aurora detention facility. Hopefully a judge will prompt them to come clean.”

Advocates for immigrant rights also praised the AG for filing the suit.

“We knew it was a long time coming,” said Andrea Loya, the executive director of Casa de Paz. “There is still a lot of frustration around the lost credibility that our health department allowed by not issuing this public health order sooner when they knew it was the needed step. And that GEO would likely not come forward willingly with this information.”

“GEO is a private company that cannot exist outside of the law, particularly when it comes to the medical neglect of our neighbors,” said Miriam Ordoñez, Immigrants Rights Program Coordinator of the American Friends Services Committee. “This lawsuit comes after weeks of pressure and is a step in upholding our state laws and holding GEO accountable for their actions.”

Candidate comments

A spokesman for Victor Marx, Weiser’s Republican opponent, provided a statement.

“Victor believes protecting the health and safety of Coloradans comes first,” said spokesman Buddy Jericho, via email. “If a facility operating in Colorado has a confirmed case of a serious communicable disease, the appropriate public health authorities need the information necessary to determine whether employees, detainees, or members of the surrounding community may have been exposed.”

At the same time, he said, the dispute is now in active litigation, and “the court should determine whether GEO violated Colorado law and whether the state's demands were lawful. We shouldn't prejudge those questions based on allegations from either side.”

“Victor supports enforcing our immigration laws, but enforcing immigration law and protecting public health are not competing priorities. Colorado should do both,” said Jericho, a consultant for Marx.

CPR reached out to other members of Colorado’s congressional delegation for reaction, including Republican Reps. Lauren Boebert and Gabe Evans. They have not yet responded.
